understand.concept: The threading module runs multiple threads within one process. Threads are useful for overlapping I/O-bound operations that spend time waiting. start begins a thread and join waits for it to finish. Threads share process memory, so shared mutable state must be protected when concurrent access can cause inconsistent results.
understand.whyItMatters: Threading can improve responsiveness and throughput for workloads dominated by waiting on I/O.
understand.analogy: Threads are several workers sharing one workshop, each able to make progress while another waits for a delivery.
understand.analogyLimit: In standard CPython builds, the GIL traditionally limits parallel execution of Python bytecode in threads; threads are not a general solution for CPU-bound speedups, and free-threaded builds have different characteristics.
understand.summary: Threading and I/O-Bound Concurrency develops advanced concurrency and performance skills.

explain.narrative:
## Coordinate threads safely
Create a `threading.Thread` with a target function, call `start()` and then `join()` when the result is needed. Threads share memory, so protect shared mutable state with locks or use thread-safe queues. Prefer high-level executors for many independent tasks.

Threads are commonly useful for I/O-bound tasks. For CPU-bound workloads, evaluate multiprocessing or other approaches based on the Python build and workload. Avoid relying on incidental execution order between threads.

examples.title: Create and join a thread
examples.code:
import threading
results = []
def work(): results.append('done')
thread = threading.Thread(target=work)
thread.start(); thread.join()
print(results)
examples.explanation: join ensures the worker has finished before the main thread reads results.

examples.title: Inspect thread identity
examples.explanation: The main program runs in the main thread.

examples.title: Protect a counter with a lock
examples.explanation: A lock protects the shared counter update from concurrent access.

examples.title: Check a thread's completion state
examples.code:
import threading
thread = threading.Thread(target=lambda: None)
thread.start(); thread.join()
print(thread.is_alive())
examples.explanation: is_alive reports whether the thread is still running.

examples.title: Use a thread name
examples.code:
import threading
thread = threading.Thread(target=lambda: None, name='worker-1')
print(thread.name)
examples.explanation: Named threads are easier to identify in diagnostics.
